title: Arjuna drops his bow
hookLine: the greatest archer's hands shake and his bow slips, Krishna answers with karmany eva, and the Hindu habit of offering the work
carry: karma yoga: do the work, offer it to Krishna
tomorrow: Jagannath means lord of the world. so why does he leave his temple?
last: ATMAN AND BRAHMAN: ONE, OR TWO?

cards: Feel it in the body first. The mouth goes dry. The legs go weak.

The skin burns. The hair stands up on the arms. That's how the Bhagavad Gita describes Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age, standing between two armies, looking across at teachers and cousins he's about to fight.
His bow, Gandiva, slips out of his hand. He sits down in his chariot. He says he won't fight.
And Krishna, driving his chariot, starts to answer.

teach.b: In chapter two, Krishna gives him one of the most quoted lines in the Gita. It opens: karmany eva. A dictionary won't list karmany.
That's sandhi: undo the join. Karmani, in action, ends in i. Eva, alone, begins with e.
Before a different vowel, the mouth slides the i into a y, and Sanskrit writes the slide down. Karmani eva: in action alone.
The whole line: your right is to action alone, never to its fruit. Don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't fall in love with doing nothing either. This is karma yoga, the yoga of action.
It isn't don't care. Arjuna still has to pick up the bow and do his duty, his dharma, fully. What he lets go of is his grip on how it turns out.
And later the Gita takes it one step further: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, Krishna says, do it as an offering to me.
That's why, in many Hindu homes, especially in the south, people finish a task, a meal, a prayer, with three words: Sri Krishnarpanam astu.

teach.h: DO THE WORK. OFFER IT TO KRISHNA.
teach.b: May this be offered to Krishna. The work is yours. The fruit is his.
Many teachers read Arjuna's story this way: the hands steady once the outcome is no longer yours to carry.

how: Many Hindus, especially in South India, end a task, a meal or a prayer with 'Sri Krishnarpanam astu' or 'sarvam Krishnarpanam', offering the act to Krishna, the habit the Gita's teaching on action gives words to.

o: waiting to act until you're sure it will work
acting fully, and offering the result to Krishna
not caring how things turn out, so you never try too hard

games.q: on the chariot — tap the pairs.
p: the archer whose bow slips from his hand
act fully, let go of the fruit
may this be offered to Krishna

s: the Gita tells Arjuna to stop caring and do nothing
his right is to action; he's told not to cling to doing nothing either.
the Gita says whatever you do, eat or give can be offered to Krishna
that's why many Hindus end a task with Sri Krishnarpanam astu.
karmany is a word you can look up in a Sanskrit dictionary
it's karmani, in action, with its i turned into y before eva.

games.q: a friend says the Gita's 'not the fruit' line means you shouldn't bother studying for the exam. what does the teaching actually say?
o: study fully, that's your part; offer the result and stop clutching it.
she's right: results don't matter, so effort doesn't either.
only study if you're sure you'll get the grade.
games.why: karma yoga: your right is to the action, never to the fruit, and not to doing nothing. Arjuna still fights; he lets go of the outcome, and offers the work to Krishna.

practice: Notice where your body is holding a result you're waiting for: a tight jaw, a knot in the stomach, shoulders up. Name the task behind it.

Now do what Arjuna was asked to do: give it your full effort in your mind, then set the outcome down. If you pray, say quietly, Sri Krishnarpanam astu. If you don't, say, the work is mine, the result isn't.
Let the shoulders drop, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: today, i turning into y before a different vowel, so karmani eva, in action alone, comes out karmany eva.

orig.note: Sanskrit: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, your right is to action alone; Bhagavad Gita 2.47. karmaṇi + eva, with the i turned into y.

carryVoice: For the road: karma yoga. Do the work, offer it to Krishna. Arjuna picked up the bow again. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.28–30, 1.47 (Arjuna's mouth dries, limbs fail, hair stands on end, skin burns, Gandiva slips from his hand; he sits down in the chariot)
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 (karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana / mā karmaphalahetur bhūr mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 (whatever you do, eat, offer, give or practice, do it as an offering to me)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.77 (iko yaṇ aci: i, u and kin become y, v and kin before an unlike vowel)
Sri Krishnarpanam astu / sarvam Krishnarpanam (offering an act to Krishna)
